Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

imagine verb

picture in the mind

also picture, fancy, just imagine, picture to oneself

classical

Cic. Mil. 79: fingite animīs
Cic. N.D. 3.47: quae cōgitātiōne nōbīsmet ipsīs possumus fingere

fingō, fingere, fīnxī, fictum

verb, third conjugation; with animō or cōgitātiōne, or an accusative and infinitive

imagine, picture in the mind

The verb of shaping clay or wax, said of the mind: animō fingere, cōgitātiōne fingere. The same verb puts a case (see suppose) and makes believe (see pretend).

Other words

  • ante oculōs pōnere — picture, call up (literally, set before the eyes)

    phrase, with pōnō · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 2.115: pōne ante oculōs laetitiam senātūs

  • imāginor, imāginārī, imāginātus sum — picture to oneself, fancy

    also used · classical · Quint. 9.2.41 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 331

    Post-Augustan (Quintilian, Pliny, Tacitus: Lewis & Short); Traupman’s word for “imagine” (p. 331).

Examples

  • fingite animīs — līberae sunt enim nostrae cōgitātiōnēs et quae volunt sīc intuentur ut ea cernimus quae vidēmus

    picture it in your minds — for our thoughts are free, and they see what they wish as plainly as we see what is before our eyesCic. Mil. 79

  • recordāre igitur illum, M. Antōnī, diem quō dictātūram sustulistī; pōne ante oculōs laetitiam senātūs populīque Rōmānī

    remember, then, Mark Antony, the day on which you abolished the dictatorship; picture the joy of the senate and the Roman peopleCic. Phil. 2.115

See also pretend, think, daydream, suppose, picture.

SourcesLewis & Short: fingo · Lewis & Short: pono · Lewis & Short: imaginor
